faqs_intro.description: FAQ tab page intro line under heading

faqs_q2.message: Why don't Google's own 2FA codes auto-fill from SMS?
faqs_q2.description: FAQ question about Google sign-in SMS limitation

faqs_a2.message:
Google hides its own SMS codes from messages.google.com for security. Even when you have Google Messages paired with InboxKey, verification codes sent by Google for signing into Google accounts will only appear on your phone.

This is a deliberate Google design choice. It prevents someone with remote access to your browser from reading codes meant to protect your Google account.

For Google sign-ins, use your phone, Google Authenticator, passkeys, or backup codes. InboxKey will auto-fill codes from every other sender just fine.
faqs_a2.description: FAQ answer about Google sign-in SMS limitation

faqs_q3.message: Why does InboxKey need the InboxBridge helper?

faqs_a3.message:
IMAP is not an HTTP protocol, and Chrome doesn't expose raw network sockets to extensions. InboxBridge is a small companion app that runs on your device and handles the IMAP connection locally. Your credentials stay in your operating system's keychain (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or libsecret on Linux), and no email data leaves your computer.

InboxBridge is required for every email provider, including Gmail. For Gmail, you connect with an App Password (Google requires 2-Step Verification first); for Outlook, Yahoo, Fastmail, ProtonMail Bridge, and other IMAP providers, you connect with normal IMAP credentials.

faqs_q4.message: Is my email or SMS data sent anywhere?

faqs_a4.message:
No. Everything parses on your device. There are no InboxKey servers, no analytics, no telemetry.

Emails are fetched directly from your provider via IMAP (through the local InboxBridge helper), SMS messages are read from Google Messages for web, and code detection happens entirely in your browser.

The Security tab has a full architecture breakdown if you want to verify this yourself.

faqs_q5.message: Why does Windows or macOS show a warning when installing InboxBridge?
faqs_q5.description: FAQ question about unsigned installer warning

faqs_a5.message:
InboxBridge is not digitally signed. Microsoft and Apple both show a warning for unsigned software.

Signing requires a code certificate that costs roughly $200 to $500 per year (Windows) or $99 per year (macOS Developer ID). InboxKey is a source-available project without funding for one, so the warning is unavoidable.

To proceed: on Windows, click More info then Run anyway. On macOS, the installer may be blocked at first launch; open System Settings → Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway next to the InboxBridge entry.

The source is on GitHub. The SHA-256 checksum of every release is published alongside the installer; verify it against your download to confirm nothing was tampered with.
faqs_a5.description: FAQ answer about unsigned installer warnings

faqs_q6.message: Why can I only pair one phone number for Google Messages?
faqs_q6.description: FAQ question about GM single-phone limit

faqs_a6.message:
Google Messages for web uses a device-paired session, tied to one phone number and one browser profile. Google's web interface does not support pairing more than one phone at a time.

If you need a second phone, create a separate Chrome profile and pair it there.
faqs_a6.description: FAQ answer about GM single-phone limit

faqs_q7.message: Can I add more than one email account?
faqs_q7.description: FAQ question about multiple email account support

faqs_a7.message: Yes. InboxKey supports multiple IMAP accounts — connect Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo, work mailboxes, or any other IMAP provider side by side. Each account is configured separately through InboxBridge with its own credentials. Codes from every account appear together in the popup, sorted by recency.
faqs_a7.description: FAQ answer about multiple email account support

faqs_q8.message: Which email providers does InboxKey work with?
faqs_q8.description: FAQ question about supported email providers

faqs_a8.message: Anything that speaks IMAP. That includes Gmail (with an App Password — Google requires 2-Step Verification first), Outlook / Hotmail / Live, Yahoo Mail, iCloud Mail (with an app-specific password), Fastmail, AOL, GMX, Zoho, and self-hosted IMAP servers. ProtonMail works through ProtonMail Bridge, the desktop app Proton ships for IMAP access. If your provider gives you IMAP host, port, username, and password, InboxKey can read it.
faqs_a8.description: FAQ answer about supported email providers

accounts_gm_disclosure_how_title.description: Disclosure section title: how it works

accounts_gm_disclosure_how_text.message: When a website asks for an SMS code, InboxKey opens Google Messages for Web in a background tab. It reads only the preview text of the last few messages, looking for a verification code. If a code is found, it is extracted and the tab is closed. If nothing is found within about 20 seconds, the tab is closed anyway. The tab is visible in the browser. Nothing is hidden.
accounts_gm_disclosure_how_text.description: Disclosure section text: how it works

accounts_gm_disclosure_phone_title.description: Disclosure section title: phone number rationale

accounts_gm_disclosure_phone_text.message: The phone number is stored only on this device, nowhere else. It helps InboxKey tell the difference between an SMS code and an email code. When a website shows hints like a country code, the last digits of a number, or words like "text message", InboxKey uses the phone number to recognize the field as SMS and check Google Messages. Without it, InboxKey would not know when to look.
accounts_gm_disclosure_phone_text.description: Disclosure section text: phone number rationale

accounts_gm_disclosure_know_title.description: Disclosure section title: good to know

accounts_gm_disclosure_know_text.message: There is no API for Google Messages. This feature works by opening the website and reading the page, the same way a person would. The Google Messages session in the browser can expire over time. If it does, re-pair the device from messages.google.com. InboxKey will let you know when that happens.
accounts_gm_disclosure_know_text.description: Disclosure section text: good to know

security_hero_headline_v2.message: Only verification codes. Only on your device.

security_hero_sub_v2.message: InboxKey reads verification emails from your inbox, parses them locally, and talks to nothing on the internet except your email provider. This page explains exactly what it does, what it does not do, and how to verify both against the source code.

security_read_scan_detail.message: The extension asks your provider for recent unread messages via IMAP (InboxBridge fetches messages from the server and passes them to the extension). Each message is parsed in browser memory. Only messages containing a verification code or magic link are kept in the ephemeral cache. Everything else is discarded immediately.

security_store_tokens_detail.message: IMAP passwords are held by InboxBridge in your operating system's keychain, not by the extension itself. The extension stores account metadata (email address, provider type) and the IMAP connection settings needed to ask the bridge to fetch messages (server hostname, port, and the local account ID that points at the keychain entry) in chrome.storage.local. No passwords or message contents are persisted there.

security_store_cache_detail.message: Detected verification codes are held in chrome.storage.session, which Chrome wipes automatically when you close the browser. They never touch disk.

security_perm_scripting_reason.message: Required to add the in-page autofill UI when a verification field is detected. Only injected on pages where a code field is found.

security_arch_caption.message: The only thing this extension talks to is your email provider. Inside your device, parsing happens in browser memory.
